effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative comparative case study with descriptive institutional process metrics in Table 1 (drawn from Kachenje 2017) and no inferential statistical estimates.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported (no inferential statistical estimate; descriptive scheme comparison in Table 1). Across 3 sampled water supply schemes in Dar es Salaam, institutional fragmentation, split accountability between DAWASA and municipal councils, weak enforcement of licensing/registration rules, and lack of inter-model coordination mechanisms hindered service delivery and responsiveness: maximum processing time for a new water connection application was 30 days involving 5 key actors in the public scheme (DAWASA, due to centralized headquarters finance/procurement and forwarding of bank pay-in slips from Area Offices) versus 3 days (2 key actors) in the private scheme and 6 days (3 key actors) in the community-based scheme.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 8–14, Results and Discussion; PDF p. 12, Table 1; PDF p. 14, Conclusions

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative case study appraised with CASP (design ceiling = 2). Directly documents administrative and institutional mechanisms operating on water service delivery and connection delays across the three sampled schemes (centralized DAWASA procurement/application routing, informal Wami-Ruvu water use permits substituting for utility/EWURA licensing, and Mtaa 5% revenue-sharing conflicts).

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines institutional fragmentation and political coordination across DAWASA, EWURA, 5 municipal councils, Wami-Ruvu Basin Water Office, and Mtaa committees; administrative burden/procedural steps, documentation (bank pay-in slips), fees, and up to 30-day delays in new connection processing; weak regulatory enforcement of provider registration/contracting; geographical service-area mandates and urban planning disconnects; and community-based participation.
